chapters.title: Vanity of Vanities
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 1

1The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.

2"Vanity of vanities," says the Preacher, "vanity of vanities! All is vanity."

3What does a man gain from all his toil at which he toils under the sun?

4A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever.

5The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and pants back to its place, where it rises.

6The wind goes to the south and turns around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its rounds the wind returns.

7All the streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.

8All things are full of weariness; no one can utter it. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

9What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.

10Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already, in the ages before us.

11There is no remembrance of those who came before, and of those who are yet to come there will be no remembrance among those who come after them.

12I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem.

13I set my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

14I have seen all the works that are done under the sun, and indeed, all is vanity and a chasing after wind.

15What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

16I said in my heart, "I have grown great and added wisdom beyond all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge."

17So I set my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I came to know that this also is a chasing after wind.

18For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

Notes

  • v1 "the Preacher" — Qohelet, "one who gathers," the speaker to an assembly (qahal); the Greek Ekklesiastes gives the book its name. "Son of David, king in Jerusalem" points to Solomon, though the book never names him.

  • v2 "Vanity" — hevel, the word that was Abel's name (Genesis 4:2). There it names a man; here it is a word in the sentence.

  • v2 "Vanity of vanities" — the Hebrew way of saying "the utmost vanity," like "holy of holies." Hevel is literally a breath or vapor, and it is "vanity" every time in this book.

  • v3 "under the sun" — the book's phrase for life as seen from this world, about thirty times.

  • vv4–7 — the sun, the wind and the streams go round and round and arrive nowhere.

  • v5 "pants back to its place" — sho'ef, panting like a runner.

  • v14 "a chasing after wind" — re'ut ruach, wind, not spirit; the phrase returns through chapter 6. In v17 it is ra'yon ruach, the same sense.

  • v15 "What is crooked cannot be made straight" — as in 7:13.

chapters.title: I Hated All My Toil
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 2

1I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good." But this also was vanity.

2I said of laughter, "It is madness," and of pleasure, "What does it do?"

3I searched in my heart how to cheer my body with wine — my heart still guiding me with wisdom — and how to lay hold of folly, until I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.

4I made great works: I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards for myself.

5I made myself gardens and parks and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees.

6I made myself pools of water from which to water a forest of growing trees.

7I bought male and female servants, and had servants born in my house. I also had great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem.

8I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, men and women, and the delights of the children of man — many concubines.

9So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also remained with me.

10Whatever my eyes asked for I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my portion from all my toil.

11Then I turned to all the works that my hands had done and to the toil I had spent in doing them, and indeed, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no gain under the sun.

12So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.

13Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness.

14The wise man has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I perceived that one fate befalls them all.

15So I said in my heart, "What befalls the fool will befall me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" I said in my heart that this also is vanity.

16For of the wise as of the fool there is no remembrance forever, since in the days to come all will long be forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool!

17So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a chasing after wind.

18I hated all my toil at which I toil under the sun, since I must leave it to the man who will come after me,

19and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.

20So I turned and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil at which I had toiled under the sun,

21because there is a man whose toil is done with wisdom and knowledge and skill, and he must leave it as a portion to a man who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.

22What does a man get from all his toil and the striving of his heart at which he toils under the sun?

23For all his days are pain, and his business is vexation; even at night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.

24There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink and let his soul see good in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God,

25for who can eat or who can have enjoyment apart from me?

26For to the man who is good in His sight He has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner He has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to the one who is good in God's sight. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

Notes

  • vv1–11 — the king's experiment: pleasure, wine, building, gardens, servants, treasure, music. He had everything, and found "no gain under the sun."

  • v8 "many concubines" — shiddah veshiddot, words found only here; the meaning is uncertain, and "chests" or "cupbearers" have been proposed.

  • v12 "what can the man do who comes after the king?" — no successor can go further; the line is hard in the Hebrew.

  • v14 "one fate" — miqreh, what happens, chance, here death, which comes to wise and fool alike (3:19; 9:2–3).

  • v20 "gave my heart up to despair" — leya'esh, to give up hope.

  • v24 "There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink" — the first of the book's refrains of simple joy (3:12–13, 22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7), received as a gift "from the hand of God."

  • v25 "apart from me" — the Hebrew is followed: who can enjoy more than the Preacher could? The Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts read "apart from Him."

  • v26 "the one who is good in His sight… the sinner" — "sinner" (chote) may mean one who misses the mark, the one God does not favor.

chapters.title: A Time for Everything
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 3

1For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:

2a time to be born, and a time to die;
a time to plant, and a time to uproot what is planted;

3a time to kill, and a time to heal;
a time to break down, and a time to build up;

4a time to weep, and a time to laugh;
a time to mourn, and a time to dance;

5a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together;
a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;

6a time to seek, and a time to lose;
a time to keep, and a time to cast away;

7a time to tear, and a time to sew;
a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;

8a time to love, and a time to hate;
a time for war, and a time for peace.

9What gain has the worker from that at which he toils?

10I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

11He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put eternity in their hearts, yet so that man cannot find out the work that God has done from beginning to end.

12I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and to do good as long as they live;

13and also that every man should eat and drink and see good in all his toil — it is the gift of God.

14I know that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before Him.

15What is, already has been; what is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.

16Moreover, I saw under the sun: in the place of justice, there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, there was wickedness.

17I said in my heart, "God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work there."

18I said in my heart concerning the children of man: God is testing them, so that they may see that they themselves are beasts.

19For what befalls the children of man and what befalls the beasts is one and the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have one breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity.

20All go to one place. All are from the dust, and all return to the dust.

21Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?

22So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works, for that is his portion. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?

Notes

  • vv2–8 — fourteen pairs of opposites, every human act given its time; God holds the times (v11; Psalm 31:15).

  • v5 "a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together" — perhaps clearing a field and building a wall, or, as later readers took it, a picture of the marriage bed beside "a time to embrace."

  • v11 "He has also put eternity in their hearts" — ha'olam, "eternity" or "the world": a sense of what lies beyond time, yet no grasp of the whole.

  • v15 "God seeks what has been driven away" — nirdaf, "the pursued": God brings back what has passed, or God takes the side of the pursued.

  • vv19–21 "one breath… the spirit of man… the spirit of the beast" — ruach each time; the breath of life that people and animals share (Genesis 7:22). Lowercase, since it is not God's Spirit.

  • v20 "All are from the dust, and all return to the dust" — Genesis 3:19.

  • v21 "Who knows" — the Preacher does not deny a difference; he says no one under the sun can see it. 12:7 gives his answer: the spirit returns to God who gave it.

chapters.title: Two Are Better Than One
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 4

1Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. There were the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them. On the side of their oppressors there was power, and they had no one to comfort them.

2So I praised the dead who are already dead more than the living who are still alive.

3But better than both is he who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.

4Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

5The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.

6Better is one hand full of quietness than two hands full of toil and a chasing after wind.

7Again I saw vanity under the sun:

8one man who has no other, neither son nor brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches. "For whom am I toiling and depriving my soul of good?" This also is vanity and an unhappy business.

9Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.

10For if they fall, one will lift up his companion. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has no one to lift him up!

11Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone?

12Though a man may overpower one who is alone, two will stand against him — and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

13Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take warning.

14For he came out of prison to reign, though in his kingdom he had been born poor.

15I saw all the living who walk under the sun, with that second youth who would stand in his place.

16There was no end of all the people, of all those whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

Notes

  • v1 "they had no one to comfort them" — said twice, as the Hebrew does.

  • v5 "eats his own flesh" — the idle man destroys himself; v6 gives the balance between laziness and endless toil.

  • v8 "his eyes" — the read form, singular eino; the written form plural. The Hebrew moves into the man's own question without "he says."

  • vv9–12 — the worth of a companion, at work, in a fall, in the cold, against an attacker; "a threefold cord," where two become three.

  • vv13–16 — a story of a youth who rose from prison to the throne and was forgotten in turn; the Hebrew does not say who.

  • v16 and Hebrew 4:17 — the Hebrew counts one more verse in this chapter; the English numbering, which begins chapter 5 with it, is followed, so it is rendered as 5:1.

chapters.title: Let Your Words Be Few
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 5

1Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.

2Do not be rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth; therefore let your words be few.

3For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.

4When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for He has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow.

5It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay.

6Do not let your mouth lead your flesh into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?

7For when dreams increase, so do vanities and many words; but fear God.

8If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for one high official watches over another, and there are higher ones over them.

9But the gain of a land is in everything: a king for a cultivated field.

10He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with income. This also is vanity.

11When goods increase, those who eat them increase, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes?

12Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep.

13There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches kept by their owner to his hurt,

14and those riches were lost in an unhappy business, and he fathered a son, but there is nothing in his hand.

15As he came from his mother's womb, naked he shall go again as he came, and he shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.

16This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain has he who toils for the wind?

17Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness, in much vexation and sickness and anger.

18What I have seen to be good and fitting is this: to eat and drink and see good in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his portion.

19Also, every man to whom God has given riches and possessions and power to eat of them, to accept his portion and to rejoice in his toil — this is the gift of God.

20For he will not much remember the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.

Notes

  • v1 and Hebrew 4:17 — the Hebrew places this verse at the end of chapter 4 and counts the rest of the chapter one lower (English 5:2 = Hebrew 5:1). The English numbering is followed. "To draw near to listen" — to listen is to obey (1 Samuel 15:22).

  • v2 "let your words be few" — compare Matthew 6:7.

  • vv4–5 "When you vow a vow to God" — nearly the words of Deuteronomy 23:21–23.

  • v6 "before the messenger" — mal'akh; likely the priest or temple officer who received the vow (Malachi 2:7 calls the priest the messenger of the LORD of hosts). The Greek reads "before God." "A mistake" — shegagah, the unintentional sin of Leviticus 4 and Numbers 15:22–29.

  • v7 "vanities" — havalim, the plural of hevel.

  • v8 "one high official watches over another" — each official answers to one above him; the abuse goes up the chain, or the chain hides it.

  • v9 — the Hebrew is obscure. It may mean that a king is a gain to a land under cultivation, or that even a king depends on the field.

  • v15 "naked he shall go again as he came" — Job 1:21; 1 Timothy 6:7.

  • vv18–20 — eating, drinking and joy in one's toil as God's gift, as in 2:24 and 3:13. "Keeps him occupied" — ma'aneh, God "answers" him or keeps him busy with joy.

chapters.title: Like a Shadow
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 6

1There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:

2a man to whom God gives riches and possessions and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to eat of it, but a stranger eats it. This is vanity and a grievous sickness.

3If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with good, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.

4For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered.

5Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything; this one has more rest than that one.

6Even if he lives a thousand years twice over, yet sees no good — do not all go to one place?

7All the toil of man is for his mouth, and yet the soul is not filled.

8For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? What has the poor man who knows how to walk before the living?

9Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the soul. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

10Whatever has been has already been named, and it is known what man is, and he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he.

11For there are many words that increase vanity. What advantage is that to man?

12For who knows what is good for man in life, the few days of his life of vanity, which he spends like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?

Notes

  • v2 "a stranger eats it" — nokhri, a foreigner or an outsider; one man gathers and another enjoys (compare 2:18–21).

  • v3 "a hundred children… no burial" — many children and long life were counted the greatest blessings; to lie unburied was the worst disgrace (Jeremiah 22:19). "A stillborn child" — nefel, as in Job 3:16 and Psalm 58:8.

  • vv4–5 "it" — the stillborn child, which never sees the sun and has more rest than the man of v3.

  • vv7, 9 "the soul" — nefesh, which also means the throat and the appetite: the toil goes into the mouth and the hunger stays; "the wandering of the soul" is desire that roams after what it does not have.

  • v10 "what man is" — adam, the name given to the man taken from the ground (adamah, Genesis 2:7). "One stronger than he" — likely God (Job 9:32).

  • v12 "like a shadow" — Psalm 144:4; Job 14:2; 1 Chronicles 29:15.

speech.text: Ecclesiastes 6
There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:

a man to whom God gives riches and possessions and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to eat of it, but a stranger eats it. This is vanity and a grievous sickness.

If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with good, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.
For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered.
Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything; this one has more rest than that one.

chapters.title: Better Is the End of a Thing
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 7

1A good name is better than precious oil, and the day of death than the day of one's birth.

2It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart.

3Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made better.

4The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.

5It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than for a man to hear the song of fools.

6For like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This also is vanity.

7For oppression makes a wise man mad, and a bribe destroys the heart.

8Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.

9Do not be quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the bosom of fools.

10Do not say, "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not from wisdom that you ask about this.

11Wisdom is good with an inheritance, and an advantage to those who see the sun.

12For wisdom is a shelter as money is a shelter, and the gain of knowledge is that wisdom gives life to those who have it.

13Consider the work of God: who can make straight what He has made crooked?

14In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him.

15In my days of vanity I have seen everything: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who lives long in his evil.

16Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?

17Do not be overly wicked, and do not be a fool. Why should you die before your time?

18It is good that you take hold of this, and from that also do not withhold your hand, for the one who fears God will come out with both of them.

19Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city.

20Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.

21Also, do not take to heart all the words that are spoken, or you may hear your servant cursing you.

22For your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others.

23All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me.

24That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out?

25I turned, I and my heart, to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the sum of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the foolishness that is madness.

26I find something more bitter than death: the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net and whose hands are fetters. He who is good in God's sight escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her.

27"See, this is what I found," says the Preacher, "adding one thing to another to find the sum,

28which my soul still seeks, but I have not found. One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found.

29See, this alone I found: that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes."

Notes

  • v1 "A good name is better than precious oil" — shem and shemen, a play of sound. Oil belongs to feasting and joy; a name is what remains after death.

  • v3 "Sorrow" — ka'as, the same word as "anger" in v9 and "vexation" in 1:18 and 5:17.

  • v6 "the crackling of thorns under a pot" — sirim and sir, another play of sound: a loud, quick blaze that cooks nothing.

  • v13 "who can make straight what He has made crooked?" — the saying of 1:15, now with God as the one who made it so.

  • vv16–18 "Do not be overly righteous" — a warning against a show of righteousness and a wisdom that claims too much; the one who fears God keeps both warnings (v18).

  • v20 — 1 Kings 8:46; Paul gathers this with the Psalms in Romans 3:10–12.

  • vv25, 27, 29 "the sum… schemes" — cheshbon, "reckoning," and chishshevonot, "devices": the Preacher sought the true account of things; mankind has invented many schemes.

  • v27 "says the Preacher" — the verb is feminine only here. Qohelet is a feminine form, a title for an office ("one who assembles"), elsewhere used with masculine verbs. With the letters divided differently it reads "says the Preacher" with the article, as in 12:8.

  • v28 "One man among a thousand" — adam, here a man as against a woman. The Preacher reports his own search; v29 lays the fault on all mankind together.

chapters.title: The King's Command
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 8

1Who is like the wise man? Who knows the meaning of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.

2As for me: keep the king's command, because of the oath of God.

3Do not be hasty to go from his presence; do not stand in an evil matter, for he does whatever he pleases.

4Since the word of a king is power, who may say to him, "What are you doing?"

5Whoever keeps the commandment will know no evil thing, and the heart of a wise man knows the time and the way.

6For there is a time and a way for every matter, though the evil of man lies heavy on him.

7For he does not know what will be, for who can tell him how it will be?

8No man has power over the breath to hold back the breath, and there is no power over the day of death; there is no discharge in war, and wickedness will not rescue its masters.

9All this I saw as I applied my heart to all the work that is done under the sun, a time when man has power over man to his hurt.

10Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to come and go from the holy place, and they were forgotten in the city where they had done such things. This also is vanity.

11Because the sentence against an evil deed is not carried out quickly, the heart of the children of man is fully set in them to do evil.

12Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and lives long, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, who fear before Him.

13But it will not be well with the wicked, nor will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.

14There is a vanity that is done on the earth: there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.

15So I commended joy, for man has nothing better under the sun than to eat and drink and be glad, and this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.

16When I applied my heart to know wisdom and to see the business that is done on earth — for neither by day nor by night do one's eyes see sleep —

17then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man toils in seeking, he will not find it out; even if the wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.

Notes

  • v1 "makes his face shine" — as in the blessing of Numbers 6:25; wisdom softens a hard look.

  • v2 "As for me" — ani, "I," stands alone at the head of the verse; many supply "I say." "The oath of God" — an oath of loyalty to the king sworn before God (2 Kings 11:17; 1 Chronicles 29:24).

  • v4 "who may say to him, 'What are you doing?'" — the words said of God in Job 9:12 and Daniel 4:35.

  • vv5–6 "the time and the way" — et umishpat; the wise heart waits for the right moment and manner.

  • v8 "the breath" — ruach, breath or wind or spirit; beside "the day of death" it is likely the breath of life (3:19; 12:7). "No discharge in war" — no one is released from this battle (compare the releases of Deuteronomy 20:5–8).

  • v10 — the Hebrew is hard. "Forgotten" is yishtakkechu; the Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts read yishtabbechu, "praised": the wicked were honored in the city where they had done such things.

  • v11 "sentence" — pitgam, a Persian word, also in Esther 1:20.

  • vv12–13 "I know that it will be well with those who fear God" — the Preacher holds to this though he has seen the opposite (v14; 7:15).

  • v15 "So I commended joy" — as in 2:24, 3:12–13, 3:22 and 5:18–20.
